title: Toward a Perceptual Theory of Transparency
authors: Manish Singh and Barton L. Anderson, 2002
central_proposition: The visual system initiates percepts of transparency and assigns surface attributes based on relative Michelson contrast and figural grouping, systematically deviating from Metelli's episcotister model by employing layered surface representations and incomplete discounting of underlying luminance.

concept_definitions.name: Transparency
concept_definitions.definition: The visual perception of one surface seen through another, involving the decomposition of local image intensity into multiple surfaces in depth.

concept_definitions.name: Scission
concept_definitions.definition: The process by which the visual system splits image intensities into multiple contributions, encompassing transparency as a special case.

concept_definitions.name: Balanced Transparency
concept_definitions.definition: A condition where the transparent layer is homogeneous in both transmittance and reflectance.

concept_definitions.name: Unbalanced Transparency
concept_definitions.definition: A condition where the transparent layer is not homogeneous in transmittance and reflectance, or where these attributes change smoothly.

concept_definitions.name: Michelson Contrast
concept_definitions.definition: A measure of contrast defined as (Lmax - Lmin) / (Lmax + Lmin), where Lmax and Lmin are the maximum and minimum luminances in a region.

concept_definitions.name: Luminance Range
concept_definitions.definition: The difference between the maximum and minimum luminances in a region (Lmax - Lmin).

concept_definitions.name: Effective Luminance (F)
concept_definitions.definition: An additive term in Metelli's equations, F = (1-α)T, proposed by Gerbino et al. (1990) as a predictor of lightness.

concept_definitions.name: Generic View
concept_definitions.definition: An interpretation of image data that is stable and non-accidental, implying that small changes in viewpoint do not lead to large qualitative changes in the image structure.

concept_definitions.name: Textural Continuity Modulo Blurring
concept_definitions.definition: A figural criterion for transparency where the boundary between low-contrast and high-contrast textured regions becomes imperceptible if the low-contrast region's contrast is uniformly increased to match the high-contrast region, allowing for blurring effects from translucent filters.

argument_structure: The paper begins by reviewing Metelli's episcotister model of transparency and its perceptual predictions. It then highlights Metelli's own observations and other empirical evidence that suggest fundamental shortcomings of the model. The authors extend the generative model to accommodate textured backgrounds and unbalanced transparency. Three experiments are presented, demonstrating systematic deviations from Metelli's predictions regarding transparency initiation, perceived transmittance, and lightness assignment. These empirical findings are used to construct a new perceptual theory that emphasizes Michelson contrast and layered surface representations, and to explain related phenomena like contrast-contrast illusions.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The visual system decomposes image luminance into separate layers (scission) when specific image properties are met. This decomposition is initiated by changes in Michelson contrast across aligned contours or groupable textures, rather than luminance range. Once scission occurs, the perceived transmittance of the transparent layer is assigned based on the relative Michelson contrast between the transparent region and its surround. The perceived lightness of the transparent layer results from an incomplete discounting of the luminance contributions from the underlying surface, biasing judgments towards the mean luminance of the transparent region itself. This layered representation also explains phenomena like contrast-contrast illusions by attributing parts of the luminance to different layers.

findings.consequent: Perceived transmittance of the transparent surface
findings.mechanism: The visual system uses Michelson contrast (not luminance range) to assign surface transmittance, with matches being linear functions of mean luminance.

findings.quote: the critical variable that the visual system uses to assign surface transmittance is Michelson contrast, not luminance range.

findings.antecedent: Transparent surface darkening the underlying surface
findings.mechanism: The magnitude of overestimation is directly proportional to the extent the transparent surface decreases mean luminance of the underlying surface.

findings.quote: Observers systematically overestimate the transmittance of darkening transparent surfaces

findings.antecedent: Transparent surface lightening the underlying surface
findings.mechanism: The magnitude of underestimation is directly proportional to the extent the transparent surface increases mean luminance of the underlying surface.

findings.quote: they systematically underestimate the transmittance of lightening transparent surfaces.

findings.antecedent: Visual system attempting to estimate lightness of a transparent layer
findings.mechanism: Observers only incompletely discount the contributions of the underlying surface, leading to a strong bias toward the mean luminance in the region of transparency.

findings.antecedent: Image region with lowered Michelson contrast (relative to adjoining regions)

findings.mechanism: The visual system prioritizes Michelson contrast over luminance range for transparency initiation, contradicting Metelli's magnitude constraint.

findings.mechanism: This criterion ensures consistency with a generic view of the underlying surface continuing behind a transparent layer, even when translucent layers scatter light and blur edges.

findings.mechanism: Transparency leads to a layered surface representation where part of the luminance/darkness of a region is attributed to an underlying layer, making the transparent region appear lighter/darker.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Perceived transmittance of a transparent layer will be directly proportional to the Michelson contrast in the transparent region relative to the surround, independent of mean luminance.
Lightness judgments of a transparent layer will show incomplete discounting of the underlying surface, biasing towards the mean luminance of the transparent region itself.
Percepts of transparency will be initiated when Michelson contrast is lowered in a region, even if luminance range is not, but not when luminance range is lowered and Michelson contrast is increased.
The contrast-contrast illusion will be explained by the visual system attributing parts of luminance to underlying layers due to transparency perception, rather than solely by lateral inhibition.
Textural continuity, even with blurring effects from translucent layers, will be a sufficient figural condition for perceptual scission.
bridge_warrants: The proposed transparency theory provides a computational rationale for the contrast-contrast illusion, explaining its sensitivity to spatial frequency, orientation, and phase, and predicting the correct sign of the effect where lateral inhibition fails.
Transparency perception modulates brightness by attributing parts of luminance to underlying layers, causing the transparent object itself to appear darker or lighter.

The theory suggests that perceived color contrast, rather than absolute differences in physically defined color space, is the critical variable for computing perceptual transparency in the chromatic domain.
methodological_critiques: Metelli's episcotister model did not allow for separate measurements of transmittance and lightness, relied on reflectance values instead of luminance, assumed balanced transparency, and used four-intensity displays which are less robust and nongeneric.
Lateral inhibition accounts for contrast-contrast are incomplete, failing to describe the phenomenology of perceived transparency and predicting the incorrect sign for White's illusion.
Beck et al. (1984) did not test Metelli's magnitude constraint in terms of lightness values and made problematic assumptions about lightness computation and the filter model.
Gerbino et al. (1990)'s 'effective luminance' failed to capture qualitative trends in lightness matching and assumed Metelli's transmittance prediction without explicit testing.
model_structure: The paper proposes a set of principles for a perceptual theory of transparency, rather than a single formal mathematical model. It describes how the visual system computes transparency by using Michelson contrast as a critical image variable to initiate image decomposition into layered surface representations. These layered representations then influence the assignment of perceived surface attributes like transmittance and lightness, and explain related phenomena such as apparent contrast illusions.
limitations: The current theory primarily addresses light-transmitting properties of transparent layers and does not fully account for light-scattering properties of translucent media, although it suggests blur as an additional cue.
The initial generative model assumes 'balanced transparency' (homogeneous layers), though the paper extends it to 'locally balanced' and discusses 'unbalanced transparency'.

paper_metadata.title: Beyond Mood and Atmosphere: a Conceptual History of the Term Stimmung
paper_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Beyond Mood and Atmosphere: a Conceptual History of the Term Stimmung
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractThe last few years have seen increasing research interest in moods and atmospheres. While this trend has been accompanied by growing interest in the history of the wordStimmungin other disciplines, this has not yet been the case within philosophy. Against this background, this paper offers a conceptual history of the wordStimmung, focusing on the period from Kant to Heidegger, as this period is, presumably, less known to researchers working with notions like mood, attunement or atmosphere today. Thus, considering this period might provide conceptual resources not yet considered in current debate.Stimmunghas the remarkable feature of encompassing the entire semantic field of mood and atmosphere, insofar as both subjects and objects can literally be inStimmung.Stimmungmight refer to the state or condition of being attuned, which is understood as a dispositional state, as well as the process or act of attuning, which includes self-activating and foreign-determined forms of attuning. The word was first used for the tuning of musical instruments, but was quickly transferred to the fields of aesthetics, psychology, and physiology. This paper will focus on the contrast between the psychological canonization ofStimmungas a type of mental state, and the use ofStimmungas an untranslatable, irreducible metaphor with unique semantic force allowing for original theorizing.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: A theoretical framework explaining how the human visual system infers the presence and properties of transparent surfaces from image information.

mechanism_chain.description: The visual system processes specific image cues, such as luminance and contrast relationships, to construct a perception of transparency and its properties.

steps.from_construct: Image luminance values in a region of transparency
steps.to_construct: Perceived transmittance of the transparent surface
